title: The battle of prayer (CCC 2725–2745)
hook: distraction, dryness, lack of faith, and not giving up

segments.voice: Yesterday, three expressions: vocal prayer, meditation, contemplation. Your line was voice, mind, gaze. Which of the three came naturally, and which took effort? Day one thousand one hundred forty-six.

"Pray without ceasing." Three words in Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians. Then comes the actual attempt. A quiet room, eyes closed, the first line of a prayer. And within a few breaths, a grocery list arrives. Then an email that needs answering. Then an old argument, replayed with a better comeback. Minutes later, the prayer is still sitting on its first line. It would be easy to decide this means being bad at praying, and stop. The Catechism has a different word for what's going on, and it's not failure. Today: the battle of prayer.
screen: `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING.` → `A GROCERY LIST ARRIVES.` → `NOT FAILURE. A BATTLE.`

segments.voice: The Catechism says it plainly: prayer is a battle. Not against God, but against ourselves, against our surroundings, and, in its words, against the wiles of the tempter. It's not a sign something's broken. It's what praying is like. Then it names the troubles one by one. Distraction first. Its advice is surprising: don't go hunting distractions down. Chasing them is falling into their trap. Just turn back to the heart. And notice what the distraction shows you, because it shows what you're attached to. The grocery list isn't the enemy. It's information. Next, dryness. Times when prayer has no taste at all, no feeling, no words. The Catechism calls this a moment of sheer faith, staying with Jesus in his agony and in the tomb. It reaches for his own image, "unless the grain of wheat falling into the ground die," it remains alone. Something is happening under the soil. Then lack of faith, which the Catechism says shows up less as open doubt than in what we actually put first, when other cares that seem urgent crowd in ahead of prayer. And a heaviness the Catechism calls acedia, a listless weariness about spiritual things. And the answer to all of it is the same. Persevere. Luke introduces one of Jesus's stories this way: "that we ought always to pray, and not to faint." It's the story of a widow who keeps coming back to an unjust judge until he finally gives her justice. The point isn't that God is like that judge. The point is the widow. She keeps coming back.
screen: `PRAYER IS A BATTLE.` · `DISTRACTION: TURN BACK.` · `DRYNESS: SHEER FAITH.` · `THE WIDOW KEEPS COMING BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray through distraction. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, choose one short line, the first words of the Our Father, or just the name of Jesus. If you don't, choose your own breath. Rest on it. When your mind wanders, don't scold it. Notice where it went, name it in one word, list, worry, plan, and come back to your line. Each return is the practice, not a failure of it. The bell holds the time.
The battle of prayer. In the Catechism, the struggle with distraction, dryness, lack of faith and weariness, met by humble watchfulness and perseverance. Today's words.

Your line: keep coming back. Today, whenever your attention drifts from something that matters, a conversation, a task, a prayer, count the return as a small win. Day one thousand one hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics who struggle with distraction or dryness in prayer are usually encouraged by priests and spiritual directors to keep a regular time of prayer anyway, gently returning to it each time the mind wanders.

myth: the Catechism says to hunt down every distraction
it says hunting them down falls into their trap; turn back to the heart instead.

against ourselves, our surroundings and the wiles of the tempter.

fork.setup: you're the widow in Jesus's story. the judge doesn't fear God or respect anyone, and he's turned you away. what do you do?
fork.reveal: she keeps coming back until he gives her justice. Luke says Jesus told it so that we "ought always to pray, and not to faint."

original.note: Greek: without ceasing, unceasingly — the word in "pray without ceasing," 1 Thessalonians 5:17.

trapdoor: what you thought: if my mind keeps wandering, I'm bad at praying.
what it means: the Catechism calls prayer a battle; distraction and dryness are part of it, and the answer is to keep coming back.
what a scholar hears: the Catechism names acedia among the temptations of prayer, and grounds perseverance in Luke 18:1 and 1 Thessalonians 5:17.

notes: CCC 2725–2745 paraphrased (copyrighted English). Check: prayer as a battle against ourselves and the wiles of the tempter (2725), not hunting distractions but turning back to the heart, distraction revealing attachments (2729), dryness as a moment of sheer faith clinging to Jesus in his agony and tomb, with John 12:24 (2731), lack of faith (2732), acedia (2733), perseverance with Luke 18:1 and 1 Thessalonians 5:17 (2742–2743).
Douay-Rheims: confirm exact wording of 1 Thessalonians 5:17, John 12:24 and Luke 18:1.
Editor pass: rewrote the lack-of-faith line to follow CCC 2732 (shown less by declared doubt than by our actual preferences) instead of the script's own 'as if God might not be there.'
